utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Kay, are you ready to start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, I would like to remind you, as I did yesterday, that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning your testimony. That is to say, that you will speak the truth the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Mr. Kay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a series of questions which will be based on your interview with the Office of the Prosecutor. And the first questions I'm going to ask you about concern the planning for Operation Oluja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So if we could have Exhibit D1842.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're working from the revised version, Mr. Kay. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Absolutely. It's the only one I know, Your Honour, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, others are struggling with --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will even do one better. E-court page 169.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, on your right-hand side, a document will come up concerning a series of questions from Mr. Foster to you on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we just go further down the page. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you can see line 18 in your language, you give information concerning a meeting that Mr. Jarnjak organised with some of his assistants and heads of police administrations. And you discuss the preparation of separate units. I want to turn your attention now to a document, which is Exhibit D409. This is a document concerning meetings that were held on the 2nd of August, 1995. And the first page there lists various people who were at a meeting in the Croatian defence ministry war room, and a series of discussions were held by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us now turn to page 5 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And can you see at 1730 on the 2nd of August, there was a meeting in the minister's office. There's Mr. Susak there, Mr. Jarnjak, and yourself. And there was a discussion concerning issues between the Ministry of Defence and Ministry of Interior, check-points, refugees. There was a discussion about Operation Flash, as more places will be occupied. It can't be the same model. Military police following the front line, and civilian police entering the -- the populated areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Various matters concerning routes, highways, and Minister Jarnjak referring to reception centres, interviews: "All MUP reserve units are mobilized on the 3rd and 4th of August, 1995, and they enter the liberated regions and take over power. "The police administration will be in Knin and Glina. "The staff will be in the MUP." And someone called Lackovic will be in the information staff. Having referred you to these notes concerning this meeting, I want to ask you matters now concerning Mr. Jarnjak's statement of the intentions of the MUP that we see on page 6. Firstly, on this date, the 2nd of August, had there been any actual preparation concerning the establishment of the Kotar-Knin Police Administration?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, there was no special need, as far as I recall, to discuss that issue then, because within the context of Operation Return, the police stations were ready to send crews to return to that area irrespective of whether the return process was to take place in a peaceful manner or by having the territory liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, at this stage, on the 2nd of August, Minister Jarnjak had already in place the methods by which the MUP would take over power; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday we had an opportunity to see that Operation Return was initiated in January 1992, and that, as of that time, we began our preparations to have the police return to the area, among other things, in keeping with the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm interested in the phrase here, "take over power," which is one that has been seen elsewhere, and as to what exactly that meant "take over power"?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that this was uttered by the minister of the interior, it can mean to assume authority within the context of authority of the MUP, which directs the conduct of the police and other elements of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And is it correct that the procedure, the plan that was devised, was that after the military police had followed the military, that the MUP would go in after the military police to take over power?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But the police was not to take over power in the full sense of the word. It was there to take on the responsibility for the work that was within their remit. They were not there to take over power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can turn, now, to the next document, Exhibit D45.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Moric, concerns the records of a meeting that was held on the next day, the 3rd of August. And these notes are dated the 4th of August. And they were from the military police administration, and they were sent to you and other senior members, including Mr. Djurica of the Ministry of Interior. If you can see the front page of the document there, records from working meeting held on the 3rd of August, and they're signed by General Lausic of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I want to do is, if the Usher can go through to page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And can you see that the topic of the meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Maybe the Croatian goes back a page. Yes, that's there in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you see there that the topic of the meeting was coordination of the activities of the MUP, military police, and SIS in the period of preparation and during the planned offensive actions of the Croatian army. And we see your team there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Next page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And can you see the team from the military police. And you open the meeting, in which you refer to the fundamental principles of the operation of the police and military police in the state of war, basing experiences on Western Slavonia, and that you and General Lausic were aware of some negative experiences of the operation in Western Slavonia, and you had the joint task to eliminate problems and mistakes which were observed then. And you have to ensure full cooperation an absolute carrying out of the tasks from their scope of activities. Now, if you could just refer there to what problems and mistakes you and General Lausic had identified that were to be dealt with in the future.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue at hand are the problems. We experienced, in the previous liberation operation of Flash, that is, lack of cooperation between the military and civilian police. There was much time wasted because of that and much efficiency as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And by that, do you mean the military police and civilian police?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the military and civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At this meeting on the 3rd of August, was it clear as between you and General Lausic that General Lausic was responsible for the control of the military to ensure that they did not commit crimes?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, it is clear, based on his job title; Mr. Lausic was the chief of the military police administration. At that point in time, it was clear to both of us, as well as to the entire Croatian public by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the idea of having full cooperation, carrying out tasks within the scope of your activities, is it right, required both you and he to understand what was happening on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. We had to have reports an information from the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now turn to a document much later in time but would be worth looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D595.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's the notes of 18th of September concerning the meeting between the military police and the civilian police at Plitvice. And what we have here, Mr. Moric, are notes that were taken by the military police administration. Firstly, do you recollect having that meeting with your police officers and the military police officers on the -- on the 13th -- 15th of September at Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recollect that a meeting was held. If I remember correctly as well, it was upon my initiative. I asked that we meet there and in that composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Court has seen a document, Exhibit D594, Your Honour, dated 13th of September, which is the matter that Mr. Moric is referring to. I won't call it up. If we can just look at what was dealt with at this meeting. Perhaps if we can go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this meeting was to discuss the lack of effective cooperation between the military police and the civilian police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, it is. But the idea of the meeting was, first of all, to use the information we had until then, to look into the state of things, in general, and then analyse how to make it better. We were also supposed to agree on how to do away with the causes of such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recollect if, prior to this meeting, there had previously been such a large-scale meeting between the Ministry of Interior police and the military police in the same way?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't recall that off the top of my head. But I do not completely exclude that possibility either. There were daily contacts between those in the military police administration and my co-workers, as well as between General Lausic and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And do you know if there was contact between Minister Jarnjak and the military police administration?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure I understood your question well. If you're asking me whether the minister of the interior had contacts with the MP administration in the Ministry of Defence, then my answer would, in principle, be no. There was no reason for the minister of the interior to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can look at the next page of the document and just run through it, because we see a series of reports from the various police administrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Next pages, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we also see reports from the military police battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Next page in the English, please. And next page in the English. If we could scroll down the English; I'm trying to find -- yes. If we can go back an English page and back a Croatian page, please. Thank you. Ah, there we are. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah, and it's just General Lausic's remarks there. If could you just have a quick look at them. And the question is this, and it's follow-up to what I asked about the earlier document: Did General Lausic accept his responsibility in relation to the control of military crime?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After having seen this document, I can tell you that it was obvious that General Lausic realised the magnitude of the problem. But in response to your question as to whether he assumed responsibility, I can only tell you that he had that responsibility prior to the meeting and after that, since it had been regulated by the legal framework of both of the ministries involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And that now concludes that topic. I'd like to, now, move to another passage of your interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: E-court page 185 in Exhibit D1842, please. And for those using the revised copy, it's pages 71 of 70 -- 71 to 76. 71 of pages 107.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go down to the bottom of this page, please. And English readers can see the question from Mr. Foster: "Who was in control of Knin after the operation had been completed?" And he takes it to run from the 4th of August to the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You can see at the top of the page that is translated to you: "So you mean after the 8th of August who was in control?" Mr. Foster says: "After the 8th August, there was considerable military personnel still in that region and there was a General Cermak based at the garrison." And then he puts the question after that sentence: "I just want to know, who was the authority at that time?" Further down the page, you give an answer: "Who was in control would be everybody and nobody." As you said, there was a lot of army there: reserves, Home Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Turning to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You refer to, there was the police, military police, citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Line 10 in the English, line 14 in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Foster says: "So we have Ante Gotovina ... in charge of military operations for that area, a General, we also have another military general, Cermak. Can you tell me who was in charge after the 8th?" Line 20 in the English, 18: "In which sense, you know who was in charge." Mr. Foster gives his understanding that civilian control had been returned to the region after the date in theory. Line 28. And then he goes back to: "...two generals in the region, military generals, and a lot of military there."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He asks what your understanding was the situation there. It was clearly confused, who should have been in control, who should have been working down there. You go into the detail on page 74 concerning Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 75.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You say at line 9 in the English, 5 in the Croatian: "When you said that the civilian authority returned, you probably also referred to emissaries from the government who were sent there in an attempt to organise civil governance, civil authority in that area."

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not see this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Line 20 -- line 5 on page 75. Can you see line 5 there? Is that it there? Yes. Line 24 in the English, 28 in the Croatian: "I understand, of course, there was still ongoing military conflicts." Mr. Foster said his understanding was it was completed by the 8th or 9th. And then the next page, line 1 in Croatian, 6 in English: "We also understand that there was also reflections of the operation which required the presence of the military in the area. Lot of work for the military still, even for special police." And so we get to the point. Line 11 in the English, 15 in the Croatian: "So my question, again, is, in your view, who in practice, in de facto, who was, do you think, in control of the Knin region after the main operation had been completed?" And you go back to the original answer you gave on page 72, line -- not exactly, but in similar terms, line 31 in the English, 29 in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, page 76, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot see this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry, we've ... there we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you see there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. We need the second interview up, sorry. We're on the -- we switched ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: E-court 190. Well done. That's it. Sorry, it's probably my confusion. Yes, that's probably -- My learned friend, Mr. Mikulicic, suggests that the witness be given a hard copy, Your Honour, which might facilitate his manoeuvring through the documents. I have had witnesses say to me it is often hard to see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Might be a good aid, if the Court agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no objection against that, I would say. We can avoid the -- any confusion by -- apart from looking at the pages at the end, also to look at the previous number. We have 4892, which is the first part; 4893, which is the second part; and 4894, which is the third part as far as numbering is concerned. They have been combined and uploaded in its entirety. But if we would look not only at the page number at the end but also whether it is preceded by a 2, a 3, or a 4, that would certainly already avoid further confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But a hard copy would not be a bad idea, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mikulicic has come to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take, it, Mr. Mikulicic that you provide a clean copy from what I see. If there are any annotations in it, I would rather have a ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Perhaps there are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I don't know whether you are working from the revised or unrevised version, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is a revised version, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a revised version. But if there is a clean copy of the revised version anywhere, and if not, it may be created.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do have a clean copy. However, there is timings marked -- Timings vis-à-vis the video recording. So it's -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that would not cause any problem -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I'm not worried about any marks that there may be on it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but, of course, if the Chamber is not aware of what the witness has before him, then ... Then you are invited to provide it to the witness, Ms. Mahindaratne, and take care that you have another copy for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much to my learned friend. We're on page 76 of 107, Madam Usher, which is the second interview, 4893.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: After that, does that help?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thanks so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we're down at line 31. And as I said, you go to -- you say: "Everybody a little but then nobody." And it's about this issue of de facto control that Mr. Foster was asking about that I'm now going to ask you a series of questions, Mr. Moric. Do you recollect the President visiting Knin as well as Gospic, Karlovac, Split on the railway --

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- in what was called the train of freedom?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that was an event that took place on the 26th of August.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me? Did you ask me whether it was on that date?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah, do you recollect that it was on the 26th of August?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain about the exact date, but I do remember the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you were on a committee concerning OA, Operation Action, Knin 95, which was the title given for the security of that journey.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That particular issue concerned all the various parties concerned in security working together to provide security for the day to ensure that there was no trouble; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. If there is a document relating to this, then we could see who were all the parties involved in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're going to go through a series of documents now, relating to this, and seeing the military police, military, and the civilian police, who was making decisions, how, in effective, security was provided. So the first document I want to look at is where this is planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At 65 ter 887, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which is a record of a meeting held at the presidential palace on 20th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And If we could just see the first page of that so everyone knows what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we will be moving to page 30, which is where discussion of the trip from Zagreb to Split on the railway line starts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the Court there can see part of the planning, that there was to be a celebration, and what was behind this particular journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And then on page 31 in the English. In the Croatian, I am stuck; I am sorry about that. Page 31 in the English shows that there was a discussion made -- launched by Mr. Mudrinic: "We'll have to concern ourselves with security. We will find a solution." And Mr. Susak says: "We'll take care of that. Don't worry."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, in think that we should have the relevant portion --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- available to the witness as well, because otherwise he cannot follow your reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, this is the one lengthy document I have, Your Honour, and in the Croatian -- I don't know if a Croatian speaker can help me. I -- page 31 of the English, where Mr. Susak agrees he'll take care of security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I do not think that this is the right -- well ... no, this seems not to be the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, Your Honour. B/C/S, page 60. Thank you. Sorry, there is my fault for doing with this. But, Your Honour, I'm doing this because it's an important issue, and I want to take the Court -- much has been made of this event, and I want to take the Court through it so the Court is aware of everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- at least, should be able to follow your reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think we're now on the right page. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- therefore, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. Moric, it was only a few words we were looking for. But they're there on the page, and we do that so that you can see them. Was there, thereafter, discussions between the Ministry of Interior and Ministry of Defence concerning the security planned for the security of the President's train.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly whether there was any discussion or not. But judging by the context and the way we worked until that point, I suppose that there was such a discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's more detail here about this planning of this journey, which the Court my find important, because great significance has been attached to -- to the -- the visit. And I ask that this transcript be -- be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1849.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, this document is how long?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 54 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what is -- is it, in its entirety, relevant, because otherwise we have another --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The passages that are relevant, unless Your Honours want to see how discussions take place. You have seen concern transcripts, and if you want to see ordinary transcripts, there's ones like this. But from pages 30 until the end is reference to the train and how it comes about and how it's planned and what the purpose of the visit is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a major portion of the document, then, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So under those circumstances, I would not insist on making a further selection. Although it is now clearly on the record that it's mainly for pages 30 and the following pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what you focused on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, the D1849 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can turn, now, to 65 ter 5007.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 23rd of August from the office of the minister, signed by Mr. Jarnjak, going to the police administrations, police department, and referring to the train of freedom on the 26th of August. And saying, undertaking measures and activities following under the jurisdiction of internal affairs, we are hereby opening a joint security action of the Ministry of Interior and Ministry of Defence with the code-name Knin 95. "MUP staff will be in charge of planning, implementing, and monitoring the implementation of the measures and activities that fall under the jurisdiction of internal affairs." And if we turn to page 2 in the English, we can see the decision. And page 2 in -- turning from Knin 95, page 2 in the Croatian, that a staff is set up that included yourself. Do you recollect that, Mr. Moric?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, counsel, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this was the operative action known as Knin 95 that then went into various activities concerning the security that was to be provided; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can just look at a parallel document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to -- May this document be made an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1850.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1850 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to 2D18-1213.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 22nd of August from the Croatian army Main Staff. And it concerns employment of forces for Knin 95, with the purpose of timely and complete securing of the travel of the President. And there is an order listing the commands of Military Districts and various others who are involved. Page 2 in the English, page 2 in the Croatian, there was a requirement to coordinate and agree upon the occupation and securing of the railway line with military police units and Ministry of Interior forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we just go through the rest of the document so that people can see what is contained within it. The next page in English. Control and implementation of the order, coordination of duties. And we see to whom this document is delivered to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And is it right, Mr. Moric, that the civilian police and military police did coordinate, in relation to the security matters on this journey?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, counsel, they did coordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1851.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1851 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document is 2D00377. And this is from the third aspect, the military police administration, from Major-General Lausic, on Knin 95, dated 23rd of August. In fact, to General Lausic from Major Juric of the military police administration. And it concerns various tasks and planning for Knin 95 and who was to take part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Moric, presumably you would not have seen this document, but it is part of the strategic planning that you would have expected from the military police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a military document drafted in the military police administration and, therefore, I haven't seen it. It was not submitted to me. But I understand, on the basis of our joint work, that this was prepared at the level of management of operative activities relating to this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1852.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1852 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a whole series of documents, in a chain, relating to this. What I propose to do, with the Court's guidance and consent, because they will not have been documents that Mr. Moric will have seen, but just to take the Court through the numbers so that in an economic use of Court time the issue that we're getting to concerning de facto control and how this is relevant can be seen, as opposed to just a simple question being asked by me but can be put into a documentary context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I -- so you're not seeking Mr. Moric's comment on these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will at the end, because I will put to him the various MUP documents, but there are documents from the other agencies, such as the military. And the relevance of this, Your Honour, is that Mr. Cermak's not mentioned in any of them as having any role, and that's why this issue is being considered, as the Court might expect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now, do you want Mr. Moric to read them or to go through them or just to bar table them? It is not entirely clear what you have on your mind. Because if you want to bar table them, then we expect a short description of relevance and then a joint filing with the Prosecution. Now, if you are seeking any comment or -- from Mr. Moric, then, of course, he first would have had an opportunity to read them, which can be done by providing him with hard copies and invite him to read them over the break. It's not entirely clear what -- what you intend to do. If, at the end, your only question would be, Did you see on any of these documents the name of Mr. Cermak, then I think we could do without, because even the Chamber is able to see whether the name of Mr. Cermak appears anywhere. That -- I mean, the reading of the witness is not any better than the reading of the Chamber and the reading of the parties. So it's not entirely clear how would you like to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm going to do is put the MUP documents to the witness because they are things he knows about. They concern his subordinates. But on the way, so that the Court has the full context and to make my point, to be frank, I would -- I was going to refer to various documents which are on the list circulated by our Defence team so that the Court has the reference for them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- and then bar table them as Your Honour suggested. That was the route I was going take. But I was going to put the sequence now so that any -- if Your Honour -- I think Your Honour may be better helped by me doing that here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To follow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I'm looking at you. Finally, what Mr. Kay apparently will do is will put the MUP documents to the witness -- not MUP documents; he will just refer to them and he will bar table them, but already, in anticipation of the bar table submission, already --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- tell the Court about the existence of these documents and what they approximately are about. Any problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I have no objection to that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you may proceed in the way suggested and discuss --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just by way of clarification, we will do the normal spreadsheet for the bar table submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that' what I said. The joint filing if it will finally be bar tabled. But in anticipation to the bar table submission, Mr. Kay will already -- well, more or less briefly describe or announce them as being in assistance and to be bar tabled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I do that because it's often difficult to follow this in the transcript and make the linkage. And I hope it's helpful to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, we agreed already to do it. So that you explained that it is worth doing it, that is implied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Your Honour. The next document dated the 23rd of August is exhibited already, Exhibit D773, and concerns the engagement of forces for the Knin 95 task. The next document is from the -- is 2D00498, which we will seek to make an exhibit in the bar table, which is from the Split Military District, Knin forward command post to the 72nd. Again, concerning Operation Knin. The next one is 2D18-1197, dated the 24th of August, on Knin 95, from the Operations Group West command, again concerning Knin 95 and the various battalions and regiments -- brigades, regiments, to whom this is copied, including those within paragraph 7 of the indictment. And then the 24th of August, from the military police administration, 2D00769. Knin 95, sent to the Military District companies and battalions, including the 72nd, with their tasks for what they called Operation Goran as well. The next one is 2D00298, dated the 24th of August, military police administration from Major Juric to General Lausic concerning preparations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the next document is from the Kotar-Knin Police Administration, dated the 24th of August, which I would like you to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you can look at this, Mr. Moric. This is from a plan, security assessment, written by Mr. Sikirica, and approved by Mr. Mijic who was the commander of the Knin Police Station and concerns the security assessment being made by them in Knin for the visit of the president. You can see there what is written. Page 2, technical details of the number of -- of policemen. Page 3, again, the technical details. And at the end of the document, you can see who it was signed by. Just looking at this document, does this indicate, then, the role within this operation, Knin 95, of, at the top level, as you, as an assistant minister, having passed information and duties down the line, seeing on the ground at the Knin Police Station, the preparations being made there. Is this the correct way by which the police was using its authority?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer, could I kindly ask to be allowed to see the first page of the document again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can go back to page 1.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Counsel, this document was drafted by the commander of the Knin Police Station. He sent it to his own police administration in Knin. The duty to produce such documents per police station and police administration follows from the document issued by Minister Jarnjak, having established the Operation Knin 95 and having prescribed specific duties and tasks for the police stations and administrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May this document be made an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1853.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document is also a MUP document, 2D1812105. 1205, sorry. 2D18-1205, dated the 25th of August, 1995, Zadar-Knin Police Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You can see, on the first page, the telegram and order and security plan that this is based upon, and its implementation plan for securing the train station area in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we go to the last page, because the details of how that security was to be delivered to can be seen at the end. It's signed by Mr. Cetina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Staff of Action Knin 95. Would that have included you, Mr. Moric?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping with the initial document from the minister announcing the operation, and my answer is, yes, I was a member of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we just go back to the first page to see what security was the certain of the police, the type of things. Security evaluation, in paragraph 1: "After the military police Operation Storm, life in the town is gradually normalising, but from a security point of view the presence and activities of rebel Serbian paramilitary members are still noticed." Just as a statement there, concerning security, was that an issue that you were aware of at the time as being a security concern?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. We were aware of this. If you are asking me personally, I can tell you that I was definitely aware of certain different types of risks in that area at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we look at the second paragraph, the town being visited by various people, foreigners, refugees, inquisitive individuals, members of intelligence services from foreign countries, government and non-government organisations and bodies. Just looking at that security evaluation, was that area of security concern something you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, Counsel. I was aware of those security concerns as they had existed before that and in some other areas as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And point 3, the UNCRO base, a confluence of few hundred people of Serbian origin, among them 62 persons sought in respect of suspicion of committing crimes against Croatia; for example, humanity and international law. Is that something that you were aware of as being a security concern in Knin at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As you can see, by virtue of this official document, the regular police sector was advised of this. Therefore, I was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1854.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1854 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to the next document I want to show you, 2D18-1221, dated the 25th of August, Zadar-Knin Police Administration. Again, concerning the president's trip. A security plan is outlined. I just want us to look at this. Security assessment, extremely complex political and security situation. It refers, in paragraph (a), to paramilitary formations; (b), to mentally incompetent persons or drug addicts. If we go to the next page, outlines the operative measures, tasks of police stations. If we go to page 3, further operative tasks and who is responsible for those tasks. Down at the bottom --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can raise the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- operative technical department is referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 3 in the Croatian -- the next page in the Croatian, page 4, please, unless it's further down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Romanic is chief of the security. On this page, we can see the other tasks. Paragraph 9, control. Knin Police Station Chief Cedo Romanic in complete charge of security. Stipe Sikirica, assistant security chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Zadar-Knin Police Administration and other police stations are to whom this document is delivered signed by Mr. Bitanga, Cetina, and Inspector Vickovic. Again, this is on-the-ground police planning and issuing of responsibility. Is that right, Mr. Moric?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. In the previous example, we saw a document outlining the plans of a single police station. Here, we see a document outlining the planning for an entire police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next document which will be bar tabled, Your Honour -- May that document be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1855.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1855 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next document which will be bar tabled, Your Honour, is 2D00092, dated the 25th of August, 1995; military police administration, sent to General Lausic, and report on the tasks of the military police administration and units in Knin 95 and all their levels of engagement. It refers to the companies and battalions, including the 72nd, and describes what they were doing. The next document which will be bar tabled -- actually, no. I'm going to call this one up. D563, please. Exhibit D563. It's dated the 25th of August, 1995. It's from the head of security staff, General Cuk. And the Court will see, from the previous documents, he was in fact in overall charge of this operation. And the Court can see on the first page the details of the implementation plan of the itinerary, where the train is to stop, meetings that were held. If we turn to page 2. Chief of the Main Staff, referring to coordination of the Ministry of Defence military police, and the regular police force providing security. We can see the details. Page 3, military police administration and what their role is. Page 4, Ministry of Defence and Security Information Service, and the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we can see there the security staff formed, which included you, Mr. Moric. Can you see in that paragraph there the tasks that were to be undertaken by the Ministry of Interior, the security to be provided.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see those tasks. Those were regular, routine tasks of the police in cases when our President or a foreign official travelled throughout Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to the next page, page 5. Croatian Guards Corps. The 4th Special Guards Battalion providing the personal protection for the President. Other guards corps carrying out security. We can see General Cuk named as head of the security staff. Travelling with the -- General Lausic. And at the bottom of the page: "All Ministry of Defence and Ministry of Interior units in their areas of responsibility will be subordinated to the security staff for the duration of Knin 95." And then we can see on the last page to whom this was delivered, including Mr. Jarnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And is that how this situation was implemented, with all the different areas of security concerns operating within their own jurisdictions? The military police, civilian police, the security services, all operating according to their own lines?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. That's how it was supposed to be. That is why each ministry, within its own remit, coordinated its own organisational units in the field. This document speaks about mutual coordination and cooperation at the level of the various services and ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next document is 2D18-1216. I'm trying to finish this topic, Your Honour, before the break, with the Court's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 26th of August, Kotar-Knin Police Administration, sent to the Zadar-Knin Police Administration, concerning the security evaluation on that day regarding the travel of the President. We see the security evaluation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you just look at that, please? It says: "The state of security in the area of Kotar-Knin Police Administration is very complex due to the recent liberation of the ... area from many years of occupation." And it refers to military formations retreating to the woods and that it was necessary to additionally secure location and properties in the liberated areas, and, therefore, there is the security plan. Is that state of security as outlined there something that you would have agreed with at the time, Mr. Moric?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did agree at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And page 2, we can see that this is from Mr. Romanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that this be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1856.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the last document I'm referring to here to be bar tabled is 2D00395, dated 30th of August from the military police administration. It was the final breakdown and report on the military police during Knin 95. Goes into their details there. And in accordance with all the other military police documents and the other documents referred to, none of them refer to General Cermak at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One question then remains, Mr. Moric. In relation to your answer, when you were asked who was in control, "it would be everybody and nobody." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, the question was not specific, so I understood that it had to do with an attempt to establish who was, generally speaking, in charge principally. However, at the time, considering the legal system, but also, in fact, there was no such position. There were several persons who were the principal ones in charge but each of them in his own area. For instance, if the question was who was the main man in charge in terms of the police or civilian authorities or so on, then I could have provided a specific answer to such a specific question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's time for the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Kay, I would like to inform the parties that, as they are aware that two of the Judges in this case are sitting in another case as well, which has slowly resumed. And although we still have to consider how we will do that at the long-term, but, earlier, we took off one day from the Gotovina case, and, in turn, were sitting two days on the other case. Now, since there's a lot of work to be done in the weeks to come, the Chamber has decided that, for next week, that we would give up our session on the 11th of December, Friday, which would better fit in the programme of the Judges who are sitting on two cases, who would have, otherwise, seven sessions, and now we reduce that to six. And we do understand that this meets another concern of one of the parties as well, which is -- I take it as a side effect, appreciated as being very welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Kay, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we go back to your interview, please, Mr. Moric, Exhibit D1842, and turn to e-court page 191, page 77 of 4893. And reflecting your last answer, Mr. Moric, in fact, Mr. Foster's question: "Who was the highest authority there, in your opinion?" Just looking at that as a question, as it took up a lot of your interview on -- on this issue, in your role as chief of the fundamental police, receiving reports daily from the liberated area, was this approach by Mr. Foster an accurate approach, trying to define someone as being the highest authority?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Counsel, I suppose that, by questions of this kind, Mr. Foster wanted to elicit a specific answer the way he envisaged it, but, unfortunately, unfortunately for him, matters stood differently, and he could not get such an answer because such an answer would not have reflected the actual situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move a little bit further down the page to line 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I would like the Court to pay attention to the English at line 19 as, just looking at it, I can see a problem in the interpretation there, because I notice, from my limited knowledge, something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could just read out slowly what you said at line 16, please, Mr. Moric, "Recimo ..." if you read out that sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "For instance, I'm talking sincerely, it was never in any way clear to me the role that General Cermak had." That's what's recorded there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it seems that the "nije," which appears twice ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I won't go any further than that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was translated at the time. So there is no need at this moment to revise the transcript, because it would obscure that the words were wrongly translated at the time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you state, at line 23 in English, 21 the Croatian, was he military commander or was he a civilian administrator. 25 Croatian, 28 English: In some cases, you could see that he is dealing with civilian matters and in some cases you could see that has military authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn over the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "And I personally don't know how his role was legally defined." If I can ask you a question here. You knew General Cermak was a General; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a generally known fact. So I knew it from the general context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know to what position he was appointed in the military?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know what his position within the military structure was, apart from the fact that I was aware that he was a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you know when he was appointed to a position involving Knin?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one officially informed me about the appointment of General Cermak. I learned that from the media. And if I remember well, I think it was certainly in the first half of the month of August, to my best recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you know if he had any military role before being appointed to any position he had in Knin? Did you know what he was doing before?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel, if I understand properly, you wish to ask me whether I knew what Mr. Cermak was doing before his appointment in the military, in the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to your question is: I didn't know, nor did I notice that he had any role in the Croatian army before he was appointed to his post in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Staying, then, on page 78, Mr. Foster asked you what sort of matters you were aware that he was dealing with; line 4, English, line 7 Croatian. And at line 10 in Croatian and line 17, line 17, you refer to meetings "with my colleagues ... he was very concerned about the security condition in that area ... he insisted ... things are solved, he was concerned with ... improving general security conditions of the area ... also, he dealt with some purely economy matters, like trying to gather the cattle ... purely economical, economy matters, and on the other side, he was a general." If we can just look at that there. Did any of your subordinates report back to you that they had attended meetings held by Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember written reports, but I do remember that some of my associates proposed to me that it would be good if police representatives were present at the meetings held by Mr. Cermak with representatives of various international organisations, so that, on the basis of the presence at the meetings, we would be aware of the context, what the subject of discussion was, and what, on the basis of exchange of various information between Mr. Cermak and the representatives of international organisations, the police could possibly do in order to improve the security situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From what you knew, did Mr. Cermak have any role in relation to the workings of the police, how they operated, what they did? Did he have any control over the local police?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Counsel, when you use the word "local," do you mean civilian police?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, that's my mistake. I mean the Kotar-Knin Police Station, Knin Police Station.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Cermak formally, legally, or in fact, was not within the subordination and organised police structure; or, more specifically, he could not affect the work of civilian police either in the formal legal sense or in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many times in August did you have meetings with your police officers who were working down in the Knin area?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean how many times did I personally meet the police management in the area of Knin?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, be it Mr. Romanic, Mr. Djurica, Mr. Cetina, Mr. Cipci, Mr. Mihic. How many times did you meet the policeman on the ground, who were on the ground, in the Knin area?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I do not remember how many times I met with them; but I was in daily contact with them, and we communicated in various ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what form of daily contact was there? What do you mean? What form of communication did you have with them?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I communicated with them by using secure phone lines which are typical for the police telecommunications infrastructure, as well as through an exchange of letters, through data-protected cryptograms, and in other ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you have face-to-face meetings as well? And I'm talking here about August, September, the first two months.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember whether I had any such meetings or not, but it is more probable that I did than that I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just taking August, how many times did you visit Knin?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain that I went there once, but it doesn't mean that I didn't go some more times. But it's certain that I went there once.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And can you remember the occasion when you went there now? Can you remember what occasion that was?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember properly, I went there when the police station in Knin was opened, that is to say, returned to us, and when the staff were introduced to this work. And then, on the following day, if I'm not mistaken, the President visited Knin, and so, at the same time, I used my stay in the area to coordinate the duties relating to the Knin 95 action that we discussed quite a lot today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: During your time dealing with your subordinates - August, September - did you have any reports that they had to defer to General Cermak on matters of law and order or security?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel. Did I properly understand that your question is whether I received any reports from my associates in which they informed me that they had to - and I emphasise "had to" - contact Mr. Cermak relating to the security situation? Was that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, could I not receive any such reports because the people from the police couldn't have had such an obligation, so it is excluded that they -- as a possibility, that they had to report to General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, perhaps -- Witness, you're saying what should or could not be the case. What Mr. Kay asked is whether, as a fact, you did receive any such thing. Whether it was illegal, whether in accordance with the rules, whether it was not in accordance with the rules. So the first question is whether you did receive any reports of the kind described by Mr. Kay; and then if you want to explain why it is very logical that you didn't receive them, fine. But we should not mix up the two things. I do understand from your explanation also that did you not actually receive any such reports as described by Mr. Kay. Is that correct? Mr. Kay, could you, in your questions, if you receive such an answer, could you always clearly verify whether the witness has answered your question in a factual sense or in a rather normative sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There was a problem, I'm told, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is obviously a problem with the translation. I'm referring to the page 38 and line 20 to 22 where Mr. Moric was talking about the obligation. And he -- he said something else that is written in the transcript where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we are going to verify whether he said anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's a very important matter as well in its --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What -- as usual, what we are seeking to verify his answer, what we could do, Mr. Kay, is to read the answer as it was translated to us; then it will be translated back to the witness. And then ask him whether that is it what he said, or what he intended to say. I leave it your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, can I just go back a little bit. You asked me whether you understood my question about whether Mr. Cermak received any reports from your associates, "in which they informed me that they had to - and I emphasise "had to" - contact Mr. Cermak relating to the security situation." And I said: "That was my question." Perhaps if you could repeat your answer to that again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now, Mr. Kay, there is one other thing that bothers me a bit: You said "in which they informed me." I don't take it that you are referring to any reports, in which you were informed about anything. No. But that's how you -- how it appears on the transcript and that's how you read it just a second ago. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're getting very confused here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh -- no, let me see -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... what I'm doing, sir, is I intend to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. It is my -- I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, you were rephrasing -- you were repeating the question put to you by Mr. Moric --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- on his understanding, and in that context "me" is, Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I made a mistake. I apologise for that, because the last thing I want to do is to add to the confusion. Could you please resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will repeat the question, Mr. Moric, because we've had an issue here. Did any of your subordinates report to you that they had to defer to Mr. Cermak's authority?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one reported to me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I don't mean that in a de jure sense but as a matter of fact, that they, in fact, had to report to Mr. Cermak in any way.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how I understood your question, Counsel. They did not report to me that they had to defer to General Cermak in any way whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I hope, Your Honour, that clears up the ambiguity at page 38, line 21, for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. -- or one of your colleagues requesting to attend meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we look at Exhibit D589, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You mention meetings that Mr. Cermak went to with the internationals, Mr. Moric. We're looking at a document dated the 28th of August, 1995. It's from the Zadar-Knin Police Administration to you. It's from Mr. Tomurad, the coordinator who took over the role of Mr. Djurica. We can see that it concerns persons in military uniforms on the first page. If we look at page 2, it concerns: "I also deem it necessary to achieve an agreement according to which the chief of the Zadar-Knin Police Administration, or the Knin ... police administration ... may be present at the meetings ... General Cermak holds with ... UNCRO, UNCIVPOL, and other international organisations in Knin so as to ensure that the police are informed about all agreements and conclusions reached, which will enable them to organise and plan tasks and duties from their purview accordingly." Signed by Mr. Tomurad. Was that what you were thinking of when you referred to the fact some time ago that one of your colleagues had said that they would like to attend the meetings with the internationals?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. I had in mind this document, in which it is proposed that an agreement about this should be reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And as you read Mr. Tomurad's suggestion here, the purpose of why he was wanting this, are you able to explain?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the purpose of his proposal is set out here in his explanation; namely, he proposed that a rule should be established, that, from these levels of police responsibility, certain representatives should be present at the meetings which General Cermak held with the representatives of the international peacekeeping mission, including their civilian police and other international institutions, so that the police would be informed about the agreements reached and could organise and plan the duties from within its pursue in accordance with them. In other words, such meetings were held without any police representatives being present so that it could not be known at the local level what was the context of the agreements reached with the representatives of international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And does this statement here indicate to you that the police were in charge of organising their own work and planning their own tasks and duties, when Mr. Tomurad wrote: "... which will enable them to organise and plan tasks and duties from their purview accordingly."?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This has to do with any potential tasks and duties from the police purview which may come out of certain proposals to be put forward by representatives of international organisations at their meetings with Mr. Cermak, such as to provide security along the routes of movement for them, as well as other types of security assistance and assistance in general to their work. This was supposed to be in keeping with the previously arranged set-up between the Government of the Republic of Croatia and those in charge of the international mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, going to another issue concerning the local fundamental police, the police on the ground in Knin, did any of them report to you that Mr. Cermak was telling them not to investigate crimes?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one reported to me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did any of them say Mr. Cermak was telling them to allow crimes to happen, to ensure the Serbs didn't get to the -- remain in the region?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one of told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm just going on through the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 78, which is e-court 192 of Exhibit D1482 [sic]. Page 78 of 4893.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Line 25 of the English, line 31 of the Croatian, Mr. Foster says what he was told by his -- by the coordinators and your chief of police administration that there were daily meetings called by General Cermak to which one of them or sometimes both or all of them had to attend and report to General Cermak which seems strange, the civilian police would be reporting to a military general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And page 5 of the next page, which we're on, page -- line 13 -- sorry, line 5 of the next page, which we're on. Line 13 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "Yes, but they were never obliged to do that. They would never ... he wasn't their boss ... he could not give them orders ... so to come to meetings and to give them reports, I believe they did so because they were at the same time [sic] at the same time and they were trying to achieve something, but legally, you know, they could have told him, We don't care if you want us at that meeting; we are not coming." Were you aware, through any information you had at the time, that your officers on the ground attended daily meetings Mr. Cermak held in Knin? Were you aware of that at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had information that Mr. Cermak was holding meetings, although the information did not indicate that it was a daily occurrence. I still believe it did not take place on a daily basis. The answer I gave at that time to the investigators reflects my opinion about those meetings as they took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was there any information you had that anything about such meetings were negative for law and order?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have any such information. And the information I had was not regular in nature about the meetings themselves. I only knew that they took place, although I didn't know how frequently. From the point of view of my management of -- over the police, it was unimportant. That is why I never asked for any reports from those meetings and never received any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we just continue through the interview, line 28, Mr. Foster gives his understanding. If we go to page 80, line 1, that's interpreted to you. And we see your answer at line 6 in the Croatian, line 13 in the English. I won't repeat that, then, as we've dealt with that. The remaining passages of the interview there. I want to now move to page 84 and page 89, e-court 198.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Down at the bottom, please. Line 30 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we see Mr. Foster referring to: "... your coordinators would report to your senior coordinators that uniformed people were committing crimes, serious crimes in the region. What was done about it or what could be done about it at the level of Mr. Franjo, Tomurad, or yourself?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to the next page, please, e-court 199.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we see there that it's translated to you. Line 14 about -- you reply about the professional policemen, in the English, line 10 in the Croatian. And then line 19 in the Croatian, line 23 in the English: "And we decided to do things that could be done immediately, which are on the local level ask for the activity of the military police and on a [sic] different level for me to act." Is that correct, then, that you did receive reports of crimes happening in the liberated areas and you took steps to try and stop those crimes?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, Counsel. I received reports about crimes taking place, the perpetrators of which, were people in uniforms, military uniforms. But, as we were able to glean from the documents we used yesterday, unfortunately, some of them also wore police uniforms. It is true that, based on those documents - that is, reports - I did everything possible up to trying to come up with solutions which may cause conflict of authority, or overlaps of authority. All that in order to prevent that, or to stop it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The reports that you were getting, if you could, perhaps, explain how the system worked from down on the ground in, say, the Knin area, with the Zadar-Knin Police Administration, Kotar-Knin Police Administration, how did the information get to you at the ministry of what was happening?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information arrived following the principle of internal organisation and subordination, i.e., via mutually prescribed responsibilities. For example, the police station in Knin reported on all relevant events from their own remit, in particular, in the field of security, to their police administration of Knin-Kotar. The police administration of Knin-Kotar sent reports to the ministry. If we used the example of my responsibility, in the sense of managing the work of the basic-duty police, the reports from the police administration of Knin-Kotar were addressed to either one of the departments within the police sector or to the sector itself and its head, Mr. Franjo, or to me personally. In the police reporting methodology, an addressee is chosen, depending on the assessment of the person sending the report and to which level that report should be sent to, depending on the significance and the scope of the problem that is being reported. That does not mean, though, that if there is something wrong about the way something was reported, corrections could not be made. Additions to the report may be sought or a change in the address list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you act only on police reports, or did you act also from any information that the minister may pass to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operational management of the police is always based on the information of security trends or developments in a certain area. For me in order to manage the most relevant information was that received from the field. Of course, in the daily work of the minister of the interior, he may have a need to hear of certain reports to exchange positions or share information with his assistant, which was myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have information passed on to you by the minister, from what he knew, that crimes were occurring in the liberated territories?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Factually speaking, as the situation was at the time, I don't know how it could have been that the minister would be better informed than I was. I don't recall any such instances.
