It is also customary that, at the level of the ministers and their collegiums, no specific issues are discussed. Only security trends.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we look at a document now, Exhibit D46, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this is a document sent by you, Mr. Moric, to the chief of military police, Major-General Lausic, on the 10th of August, 1995. It is a letter. And it states: "According to reports from the field ..." and you mention Lika-Senj, Zadar-Knin, Vojnic, Vrginmost. "Cases are being noted of individual Croatian army members on liberated territory stealing ... burning ... killing cattle ..." You mention lack of cooperation. And you state: "While understanding the size and nature of the tasks that you have to contend with, we kindly ask you to take measures to eliminate these things." From the information you received about what was happening in the field, was this an appropriate method of dealing with the problem that had been reported to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I had received a report on similar issues, it would have been only logical for me to report this to the relevant address, where those who were supposed to deal with that problem were. In this instance, that relevant address was the MP administration and its chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This letter is dated the 10th of August. Did you also discuss this matter face-to-face at a meeting with General Lausic at this time?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall having a meeting with him about this information. However, we did meet frequently, and we had daily communication. In our daily contacts, the chief of the MP administration and I discussed these or similar matters which were indicative of the trends and of the direction in which events could take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he give any explanation to you as to how he was dealing with these matters?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. He provided explanations. In principle, he was a dedicated person, like myself, decisive in his intention to put a stop to such similar events. In the context of our cooperation, we never experienced a conflict in the sense that we would reject each other's invitation for cooperation within our purviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could look, now, at Exhibit D48.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a further document written by you, Mr. Moric, to General Lausic. And it concerns the reports that you had been receiving from your police stations and police administrations; of houses being burnt; people's property stolen. And in this letter, it states: "The perpetrators of these acts, in most cases, are persons wearing Croatian Army uniforms. Our information points to these persons who are formally and in effect members of the Croatian Army, but that there are also persons who are not members of the Croatian Army ... abusing the ... uniform." And you conclude that the joint work of the civilian and military police has not produced results. And you ask that another agreement on a new method of joint work in order to eliminate these problems be made. In relation to this letter that you wrote to General Lausic, what steps were then taken as a new method of joint work, to eliminate problems?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As in the previous cases when I warned about the existence of that problem, I believe my learned friend, Mr. Lausic, reacted by having ordered the units of the military police to step up coordination and cooperation with the civilian police. Based on the previous practice and having learned from our previous experiences that the military police had difficulty following the pace of the civilian police, because they were not as well educated and as efficiently organised, as well as being short of staff and not as mobile, I can refer you to my document of the 18th of August, which we saw yesterday, in which, in one of its paragraphs, inter alia, I am trying to resolve the situation by actually asking of the police force to undertake some of the jobs of the military police, thus risking a conflict of authority. The intention was to compensate for the shortcomings in our cooperation with the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At this stage, by the 17th of August, 1995, did you have actual data that you could rely upon for the conclusions as to the identities of perpetrators? Did you have a way of collecting and storing information of identities of perpetrators at this time?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Counsel, I believe that I received reports and that we have already seen that from the documents, and here I refer, in this document, to reports from police stations and administrations, because that was the chain of reporting. And it is mentioned in these reports who the perpetrators of crimes were but not by name; rather, by category. Personally I had no reason not to trust these reports from police stations and administrations; and, unfortunately, the later developments confirmed that the reports, which mention the categories of perpetrators, were correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just for the Court's purposes, the document we looked at -- the witness referred to is Exhibit D49 that he referred to as the document yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I won't look at that document now, as you looked at it yesterday, Mr. Moric. I will turn to another document, Exhibit D588. This is another document issued by you, Mr. Moric, to the heads of your police administrations dated the 22nd of August. And it refers to: "After liberation of a large territory ... the return of military units to barracks ... and after partial demobilisation of conscripts, concern quantities of weapons," referring to ammunition, mine, explosives, "were brought to the previously free territory of the country." And you assess the quantity of this material will be larger after complete demobilisation of the planned number of consequences. They could be used in breaching the peace and endangering safety, used for attacks. And you refer your police administrations to carry out tasks ordered in July of 1993. First of all, could you -- are you able to remember what those tasks were which you refer to in this document?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I do not remember. But just trying to draw a logical conclusion, I could say that these were probably tasks relating to the police paying attention in its daily work on places where public rallies were being held, when celebrations were made, and where it could be particularly dangerous if weapons or mines or explosives brought from the areas covered by Operation Storm were used. But I'm not certain that this is what it's all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is now just over two weeks after the liberation of the previously occupied territories. What problems were you facing at this time regarding crimes that were being committed? Let me make that a less general question. Were you able to see or understand what was causing crimes, who was causing crimes at this time?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crime police was in charge of processing crimes, and, as you know, in every specific case, it is only the criminal investigation that might shed light on the motives. So it's difficult for me to answer specifically to your question. But from the point of view of my remit, that is to say, managing the work of regular police, the data I found to be relevant was that these kinds of crimes were being committed, that the perpetrators belonged to the categories as noted in the earlier document, and it was important for me to monitor the trends, whether there was an increase or a decrease, in the number of such crimes. But, generally speaking, it is well known that, in principle, the crimes relating to property are caused by a will to gain something illegally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you ever in receipt of data that enabled you to conclude that this was organised, that the crime was being organised to take place?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no intelligence that would indicate that any of these crimes were committed in an organised way. And criminal investigations would have helped to establish such an information. On the other hand, in these days, as we could see yesterday, I was briefed, as was only natural by our secret services as well, and if the criminal investigations did not indicate something of the kind, then I believe that secret services would have indicated to me that there was some sort of organisation that directed crimes being committed on the liberated territories. However, more important than that was to see, as we call it, the modus operandi, that is to say, the way in which these crimes were committed, whether these were just individual acts of persons who committed those crimes, or possibly whether these were groups of two or several people but not any sort of organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Foster was asking you questions in your interview about people higher up in authority planning it. Did you have any information or any indication at the time that people in positions of authority had planned that these crimes took place?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Mr. Foster, while discussing several subjects, suggested the possible answer, but the facts are relevant. No, I am not aware that anyone would ever have considered organising such unlawful acts, nor did I ever feel an atmosphere that lead me to conclude that possibly, at high state levels, there was indifference to these developments. Quite the contrary. There was no indifference. But at the level of the ministers of the interior, the defence, and justice with whom I was in occasional contact at the time, I could see that they were worried because of such developments and that they wished that this be changed. And by the logic of the duty that I was discharging, I particularly felt personal pressure because, considering my remit of duty within the legal system and considering the previous logic, the expectations were greater, in terms of the regular police, in terms of preventing the commission of such crimes. So, in brief, I was exposed to enormous pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us now look at Exhibit D592. This is a document written by you, Mr. Moric, on the 6th of September, 1995, for the attention of Mr. Lausic. And it encloses two Official Notes in connection with activities which should be of concern to us both. You ask for measures to be taken and to be informed about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we then turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: They are notes derived from Knin -- Kotar-Knin Police Administration. In fact, they were Official Notes signed by the Deputy Chief, Mr. Gambiroza. They concern specific instances involving soldiers and what happened, and what they were doing is explained in the note. I have no need to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page, please, in the English, and -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Official Note, the second one, again, from Mr. Gambiroza at Knin Police Administration, concerning, again, matters that he had seen concerning Croatian army soldiers, what was happening, who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This matter was reported to the 72nd Battalion, and why the note was submitted. Having seen this document, Mr. Moric, first of all, do you recollect it as a document?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure which of the three have you in mind, or do have you in mind all three documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: All three. Do you recollect this instance of Mr. Gambiroza sending you these Official Notes and then you sending them to Mr. Lausic?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly, I do not remember how these reports were sent and forwarded and how they reached me. But from my letter to the chief of the military police administration, it is clear that the reports did reach me, because I'm saying in the letter that I'm submitting them to him, and I'm asking him to try to resolve this together. But I believe that if we have a look at the text of my letter --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... back to the beginning, page 1.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the second paragraph, I asked for measures to be taken to prevent such occurrences. So not just that we should try to resolve these two specific cases, but that measures be taken to prevent such occurrences; therefore, that this trend should be stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This comes from Knin Police Administration. Was this a -- a usual or unusual way of you receiving information?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was submitted in accordance with the reporting principle which I explained in my answer to one of your previous questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's probably a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Kay. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just following on to a different area now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go back to Exhibit D1842, please. And if we turn to page 199, which is where we were, and then turn to the next page, page -- e-court, 200, 86 of 107 of 4893.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We see on this page at line 5 in the English, line 1 in the Croatian language, your reference to being in daily contact with General Lausic. You refer to the Plitvice meeting. We have looked at that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, please, 201. Dealt with military police issues. Turn to page 202. Page 203 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this is the next subject, Mr. Moric, I want to turn to in your interview, so moving away from General Lausic and the military police. And it's when you're asked for why the problem went on for as long as it did. Mr. Foster mentions two military generals in the region. And you, at line 23 in the Croatian, line 25 say: "There is rather a simple answer. Can I go back to the map?" And if we turn to page 204 of your interview, we can see that you start describing the -- the particular area. Mr. Moric, why this crime could not be controlled is something you were asked in this interview. I'm going to ask you again, as to reasons you may have or be able to give, as to why this crime could not controlled.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, in the answer to your question, I should start from the general context relating to the area. It is well known that, after military operations, war military operations, there is always a certain period of confusion until all the mechanisms of authority are consolidated. Next, the size and the geopolitical position of the area in which Operation Storm took place also had a significant role. If I remember properly, I think it's 11.000 square kilometres of space, behind which there is about 400 kilometres of the state border with Bosnia-Herzegovina and including areas in which, on the other side of the border, were territories under the control of Republika Srpska. So 11.000 square kilometres is a vast area in which, after the military operation, the legal system conceived for peacetime is to be applied. One of the problems was also the factual situation following the war which was in conflict with the legal system designed for peacetime. In addition to that, various categories of people entered this area or spent some time there. There were straggling paramilitaries or members of the para-police, or they would infiltrate the area later from the territory of the neighbouring state. Then there were also the citizens of the Republic of Croatia who held the citizenship of Croatia but who were ethnic Serbs and who remained there after the Operation Storm. Then ethnic Croats who were also Croatian citizens spontaneously were returning to the area, as they could freely do that, and come back to the areas where they had not been for four years or longer. Upon their return, they would, as a rule, find their property destroyed. As I said in one of my answers to your questions today, and as one can see from the documents about the -- about the assessments of the security situation in the area made by police stations and administrations, in addition to everything that I listed so far, activities of various intelligence services were also observed in the area, including, according to the information which I was receiving from our secret services, the remaining elements of the secret services of the previous authorities in the area, and including the services of the country with which we were not officially at war but, in fact, were. So in addition to everything that is typical for areas following military operations and everything else that I mentioned, the situation was certainly such that it fostered developments of this kind. However, all eyes were turned to the regular police, because, on the basis of the legal system, it was responsible for prevention, that is to say, the general security, and prevention of crimes, including military police, which, according to its responsibility, was responsible for that, in terms of military personnel or any other persons who visually looked like military personnel until the moment when it was established that they were, in fact, not soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to e-court page 206.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: After you have described the area, you mentioned some 40.000 men would be needed to have some sort of concrete control of the area. Did the Ministry of Interior have 40.000 policemen for the liberated area?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Counsel, I believe that you wrongly interpreted one detail from my interview with the investigators, or at least it was not my intention to say so. Namely, I was not categorical in the sense that 40.000 men would have been sufficient. Quite the contrary. I wanted to tell the investigators that not even 40.000 men would have been enough. And we can easily get to this information, if we look at the typical way that police is organised in its activities. Namely, if we were to deploy one policeman on every kilometre to the area of 11.000 square kilometres because of the configuration of the terrain, they couldn't even see one another. And as I explained yesterday, if we were to work in four shifts, in which case everyone would work eight hours, then, four times 11.000 is 44, and if we burden them so as to work 12 hours a day so that they would work in three shifts, that means that we would have 36.000. So what I wanted to say was that even 40.000 would not have been enough. And a direct answer to your question, did we have so many men? Unfortunately, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. You asked for data to be supplied from the various police administrations as to what they had been able to report and investigate after your order on the 18th of August; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You could say that it was so. Namely, when it was clear that we were faced with a spate of negative events, as I said, it was clear that we had to respond to that situation, which included requests for people to work beyond the limits of their abilities, that is to say, of the powers they were invested with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to Exhibit D573, this is a response to a request for data by you in an order dated the 22nd of August. This document is from the Sibenik Police Administration dated the 24th of August, and it outlines seven topics that you had asked to be reported upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that's Exhibit D50 that caused that, Your Honour, to link up this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we can just look at the responses that were given to you. Cooperation with the police administration and police stations were inadequate. Is there any comment you could make about that, about inadequacy of cooperation between the Sibenik Police Administration here and its police stations?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I believe you meant the cooperation between the civilian police and the military police, rather than the police administration of Sibenik and police stations, as you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have, in paragraph 1 of the English translation here: "Cooperation within the police administration Sibenik and the police stations on the territory of this administration is inadequate." Perhaps could you read out so that we can -- paragraph 1 of this -- number 1. Can you read that out, in the Croatian?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, are you right. I see it now. So I apologise. This is what it says. However, I believe that this was a misunderstanding. It would be clearer if we could see the document -- my document dated the 18th, because, as far as I remember, under item 1, I requested that cooperation with military police be assessed. And then, in this document, they report to me that that cooperation of the Sibenik Police Administration and the police stations in the area is inadequate. So that was the cooperation I had in mind, the cooperation with military police, if I remember my own document properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, it seems from paragraph 2, if that is directly related to paragraph 1, that there may be a mistake in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we can see paragraph 2 there, about cooperation with the 72nd Battalion. I'm going look at this, actually, for another reason, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to page 2 of the English, and down at the bottom of page 1 of the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're looking at paragraph 7, Mr. Moric. Can you see that? 36 perpetrators of crimes identified of which five are members of the Croatian army in uniform and the others are civilians.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So five out of 36 being military or -- or HV in uniform, while others are civilians. In relation to this kind of data, how was it used or studied? What did you do with it?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is clear, from the manner of reporting, that, at the level of the assistant minister, specific cases were not analysed but just tendencies so that, on the basis of tendencies, decisions could be made about directing, prevention, and managing the work of the regular police. On the basis of such information, at my level, I made an assessment as to whether we had the cooperation of the military police to the degree that was necessary, considering the situation. And when the conclusion was that the cooperation was not satisfactory, then I would intervene with the heads of the military police. But I think that, if you allow, it is important to notice two other details in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In item 3, it is reported that there are still cases of burning, destruction, and illegal removal of movable property in the liberated areas but to a smaller extent. And I think that it is important to notice here that the problem is decreasing. And under item 6, it states that in all cases, a criminal investigation of the crimes is conducted. I am reported [as interpreted] about the tendencies here, and I am only reported about criminal investigation and processing in the context of the necessary assistance that the regular police should provide with crime police duties. So they do not report to me as the assistant minister who is responsible for the work of the crime police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We know this was in response to your telegram of the 22nd of August; Exhibit D50. And if we look at number 5, paragraph 5, we see that from the time of receipt of the telegram until today, the 24th - so that's two days - 21 on-site investigations were carried out. And it describes the type of cases. You were looking at trends. This number of on-site investigations by the Sibenik Police Administration, was that a quantity that showed they were under-investigating, or was that a high quantity, or was that a quantity you would have expected they could have coped with to investigate?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that, unfortunately, we were undoubtedly faced with a spate of negative events. When I said that, I wanted to emphasise by this formulation that there was an unusually large number of such cases. And in this context, if, in two days, we had 21 on-site investigations conducted in cases like these with life and property were endangered or other people's movable property was stolen, then it has to be emphasised that this is to be contrasted with peacetime. It was a great problem. And in this context, we were concerned, because we wondered when we would reach the level of security that would be at the normal level in areas where no military operations had been conducted. And this was an area where all of this was happening in the wake of the military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So looking at it, did 21 on-site investigations give you a figure that Sibenik Police Administration was not doing its job, or did it give you a figure that showed it was doing its job?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it looked as if they were doing their work properly under the conditions that were implying a burden that was several times higher than under normal circumstances, and one should take into account the fact that this area was just a part of the area of responsibility of the Sibenik Police Administration. It was also in charge of areas where there had been no military activity, that is to say, that were not covered by the Operation Storm, and there they also had to carry out their regular police duties and regular police work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was the territory of the Sibenik Police Administration increased after Operation Storm to include areas that had previously been occupied?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in normal times, would this police administration expect to be dealing with 21 on-site investigations in two days, or would that be more than its usual number?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This figure put into a routine police work framework in the area of the Sibenik Police Administration at the time, and concerning the type of crimes, would have occurred within a six-month period or even within a one-year period. Generally speaking, the police administration may have been able to conduct 20 or 21 on-site investigations on other types of crimes, such as burglaries, breaking and entry, traffic accidents with significant property damage and wounded or killed people in such accidents. If we take that into account, then perhaps this figure would be valid for a full month. But if we take into account these specific crimes, that would have covered a much longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's go to Exhibit D575.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is the next report from Sibenik Police Administration, 1st of September, 1995, arising from a request by you, again, for data. And we can see what it deals with in paragraph 1. If we turn to paragraph 2 of the document, we can see a comment on the VP units in paragraph 2. Lack of personnel. We can see, in paragraph 3, incidents, the type of incidents. And we can see the figure between, in paragraph 5, 22nd to the 31st of August, 48 on-site investigations carried out as a total. Again, taking that period of nine days, 48 on-site investigations, is that a lot for the Sibenik Police Administration?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For this type of crimes, that is to say, stealing other people's property and arson, this is far too many, in relation to their regular routine police work in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The capacity of the police administration to have more investigators within their criminal police department to carry out on-site investigations, was that possible to expand, to provide the appropriate police to carry out the investigations?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think my colleague, assistant minister in charge of the crime police, did so. He increased the number of crime policemen in the territory of these police administrations, although I do not recall the exact figures and which areas specifically. It is easy to see that those police administrations and stations needed any kind of assistance at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to page 3 of the English to paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You can see it in the Croatian on the first page. 38 perpetrators, eight members of the HV; rest are civilians. We see it signed by the chief of the police administration. I want to put these questions, now, to you: Could you have done more to prevent crime? Could you have done more to expand your police?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, yesterday we discussed the number of policemen we brought in from the two-thirds of the territory that was free whom we sent to the area liberated in Operation Storm. We undertook the risk of having too few in the area where there were three and a half million of Croatian citizens, also running the risk of seeing the number of crimes proportionally increase in that area. We simply weighed the benefits against the damage. We concluded that the damage in the free areas were to be -- was to be far less than choosing not to intervene in the territory liberated in Operation Storm. Hence, I believe we did our utmost. The people we sent into that territory to assist had to bear an additional burden, by having introduced the new shift change, that is to say, three shifts per day, which meant that he had to work in excess of eight hours per day. In my document of the 18th of August, I consciously opened up the possibility for the civilian police, in cases of absence of the military police, to enter the area of the military police purview. We objectively, excessively burdened our personnel. And on top of all that, we asked them to possibly overstep the boundaries of their purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could just look at another document, 65 ter 2D00485 from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, when waiting for this document, I'd like to -- I'd like to know -- have a bit more of an answer on a question which I think implicitly was put to you, but perhaps I may not have understood the answer. Mr. Kay has put to you 21 on-site investigations in two days; and from other document, it appears 48 on-site investigations in nine days. And he asked, Does that mean that the job was not done. I have not received a clear answer. You said it is far too many, and you told us that you would need at least so-and-so many days, if not a month, for doing the same job. Now, there are a few possibilities. The one is that it's a -- impossible to do 21 on-site investigations in two days, which means that either they were not done, or they were done in such a sloppy way that it could not be taken seriously, or whatever other explanation you may have. Same for the 48 on-site investigations in nine days, an average of seven a day, how many policemen were there available ... So I would like to know how you interpret this. Do you interpret this as -- well, we did it, but it must have been done in an improper way because you can't do it properly in such a limited time, or do you have any other explanation that it was exaggerated or perhaps 10 percent was done properly and the remaining 90 per cent was done properly. Whatever. Could you give us a clear answer to the matter? You said it was far too many for such a number of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you don't know, then please tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I know the answer. Then I must have misunderstood counsel in his question. I thought he was asking me whether the number of crimes and the structure of crimes in that period was much in excess to what would otherwise be expected in peacetime. That is why I said there far too many, especially in terms of types of crime. In peacetime, some of the crimes of that type would not have taken place anyhow. That was the thrust of my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I do not know whether you understood Mr. Kay's answer [sic] correctly. If so, then I take it that you have answered the question. But, then, I have added a question to the question that was put to you by Mr. Kay. But perhaps Mr. Kay clarifies what he intended to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I'm talking about is the capacity of the police administration to deal with 21 on-site investigations in that many days. Perhaps we start, first of all, with who attends an on-site investigation. Who does an on-site investigation? Perhaps you could list the people you would expect to see.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian police is duty-bound to secure the scene of crime in order to preserve any traces of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... sorry. Don't put the jobs. Let have the people. Forget the jobs; we know the jobs actually. We have other -- just tell me the people who attend an on-site investigations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And primarily the number of people which were employed by the persons reporting. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the number of people, of course, depends on the type of crime involved and the size of the location. But, in principle, when there is an on-site investigation, that involves the basic-duty police and the crime police simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, perhaps, on average, how many duty police, how many crime police? The time of the -- the type of crimes we're talking about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Take the burning of a house, as an example, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although minority and those numbered, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But -- most -- okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we use that example there should be at least three basic-duty policemen and two crime policemen plus a scene-of-crime officer or a crime technician that. That would also depend, of course, on the location and the way the crime was perpetrated, including the area size.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would the investigating judge attend?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I did not mention him, because he is not part of the Ministry of the Interior. But, in any case, an investigating judge should be called in. Under the then-Law on Criminal Procedure, an investigation is directed by a judge. And it is also clearly defined as an investigating activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah, so what I need is not just Ministry of Interior, but it's all the people who would attend an on-site investigation in the Croatian system at that time. Does the investigating judge come on his own, or is there any other official staff?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, he or she would not come alone. They always have an assistant as well as technical personnel that accompany him. In principle, there would be at least two people: the judge and an assistant who would be there for technical assistance, transport, bringing in equipment, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it may assist the Court if you tell them, now, in relation to a looting where a house has had its contents taken away, or some of its content, let's say, fridges, or a fridge, furniture; and there's an on-site investigation. In relation to, then, the theft of removal property, how many people from the Ministry of Interior would attend?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I understand your question, and I hope you understand that that depends on the scope or size of the crime, the size of the house, the number of items taken away. It also depends on the initial report based on which an assessment is made of a possible number of perpetrators. We have to assess whether a single person could take the items away or whether there must have been assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you say it depends on the circumstances; that's perfectly understood, on average. And could we go how many basic police officers would be, on average, attend a on-site investigation in relation to stealing private property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we use the example of a house, then that would be at least two basic-duty policemen and also at least two crime policemen. If we speak on average, then I would be prone to say three regular-duty policemen, three crime policemen. And if we add the investigating judge on top of that, plus his assistants -- assistant, I would say there would be three of them as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in your experience, an on-site investigation in relation to arson would take approximately how much time? From arrival of all those, until they leave. Again, on average; arson case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, speaking from experience, unfortunately, mostly in the cases of arson, an on-site investigation is made somewhat easier, no matter how harsh that may sound, because most of the traces would have been destroyed anyhow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Explanations may come later, but I would first like to have an on-average time of such an on-site investigation; arson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On, average, Your Honour, it would last between one and a half and two hours. But what would take the most time would be to ascertain the way in which that arson was committed. One would need to carry out expert analysis afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand all that. But we are focussing, at this moment, on on-site investigations, as reported, that had taken place. Same question for theft of private property. On average, from arrival of those in attendance, up till them leaving the place - and I do understand that you need time for transportation as well - for a -- private property being stolen; an on-site investigation. On average, how much time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would take longer, because one needs to look -- locate and fix any existing traces, including the so-called papillary lines. I would guess that it would take between three and four hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, please proceed. I think we're trying to find out the same information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We are -- we certainly are, Your Honour, and I'm grateful for Your Honour's assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: An on-site investigation, does that include just the work at the place, the scene of the crime, or is there further work involved in the neighbourhood of the crime within those time estimates? For instance, going to other houses in the village or in the location to see if someone is there, to speak to them, finding people in the fields nearby? Can you describe exactly what an on-site investigation is now, having given us that information?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I am not a crime expert, but I can speak from experience and try to answer as clearly as possible. It is very difficult to take an average for a standardised procedure in locations of such crimes, but frequently, in practice, such measures are needed to actually shed light on the crime itself and to detect the perpetrator. If one wants to catch such a perpetrator, one needs to undertake a number of measures and activities beyond the location itself. This includes the settlement itself, as well as going to other settlements or towns. And it would largely depend on the type of information you gather. This may entail long-distance travel even, although not frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do these average times that you've been able to give us - and we appreciate that they're average - do they include work outside the immediate area as part of the on-site investigation, or is there further time needed for other work outside the immediate area?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood His Honour's question as having referred to the location itself. That is to say, what would be the average time to investigate a crime on location and not to conclude the entire criminal investigation in order to close the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I know that you've -- you're not finished yet with this. I'm looking at the clock, however. We have to adjourn for the day. Could you give us an estimate on how much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, one session, and I will be done tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that you're going over the three sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am, with apologies, Your Honour. But we have travelled at a fast pace, I would say, in my own defence. If I should defend myself. And we've covered many, many issues which, I think - in our submission - are relevant to this case, and particularly the Defence of Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I will discuss with my colleagues whether there is any case to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, I give you the same instructions as I gave you yesterday and the day before, that is, that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony. And we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00. Because we adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow, Friday, the 4th of December, 9.00 in the morning, in this same courtroom, III.
